Micronutrients in agriculture: what they are, how they work and why they matter
Micronutrients and trace elements for farmers: the full list, what each does, deficiency signs, fertilizer types, and how to diagnose and correct problems.

Micronutrients are the nutrients a crop needs in very small amounts: zinc, iron, manganese, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine and nickel. They switch on the enzymes, hormones and processes that let the crop use nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, form chlorophyll, flower, set fruit and resist stress. A shortage of any one limits the whole crop, however much NPK is applied, and Indian soil tests show such shortages are widespread.
By Gafar Laiya and the Gujarat Bio Organics team. Updated November 2026.

What are micronutrients?

Plants need 17 essential nutrients. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come from air and water. The rest come from the soil and fall into groups by how much the crop needs. Micronutrients, also called trace elements, are needed in grams per acre rather than kilograms, but a crop cannot complete its life without them.

How micronutrients work
They switch on enzymes: zinc, manganese, copper, iron, molybdenum and nickel are parts of, or activators for, enzymes that drive growth and energy.
They make chlorophyll possible: iron and manganese are needed to form it and run photosynthesis; magnesium sits at its centre.
They make hormones: zinc is needed for auxin, the growth hormone.
They build cell walls: boron and calcium hold walls together, and silicon strengthens them.
They make flowers fertile: boron, zinc and copper are needed for pollen and seed set.
They help use nitrogen: molybdenum, nickel and sulphur turn nitrogen into protein; molybdenum and cobalt help legumes fix it.
They defend the crop: copper, manganese, boron and silicon strengthen tissue against pests and disease.

India's soils: shortages are widespread

An ICAR survey of 2,42,827 soil samples from 615 districts found 58.6% of soils short of sulphur, 51.2% of zinc, 44.7% of boron, 19.2% of iron, 17.4% of manganese and 11.4% of copper, counting hidden shortages. Many fields were short of two or three nutrients together, most often sulphur with zinc, zinc with boron and sulphur with boron. Alkaline and calcareous soils, low organic matter and years of urea, DAP and MOP without sulphur or micronutrients are the main reasons.

Indian soil figures: Shukla AK, Behera SK and others (2021). Deficiency of phyto-available sulphur, zinc, boron, iron, copper and manganese in soils of India. Scientific Reports 11, 19760. Based on 2,42,827 soil samples from 615 districts in 28 states. Read the study. The figures include soils with a hidden (latent) shortage.
Common practices that miss the cause
Applying more urea when leaves turn yellow, though yellowing from sulphur, iron, zinc or magnesium does not respond to nitrogen.
Using NPK water-soluble fertilizer as a cure-all, though most grades carry little or no micronutrient.
Spraying a pesticide when the crop looks weak, even when no pest is present.
Treating the nutrient that shows the symptom, when the real limit is another nutrient, the soil pH or the water supply.
Read why more urea does not fix yellow leaves and why a pesticide spray will not fix a nutrient problem.

What are micronutrients in agriculture?

Nutrients a crop needs in very small amounts: zinc, iron, manganese, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine and nickel. Calcium, magnesium and sulphur are secondary nutrients, and silicon and cobalt are beneficial elements.
What is the difference between micronutrients and trace elements?
In farming the two terms are used for the same group: nutrients needed only in trace amounts. Trace elements is sometimes also used for beneficial elements such as cobalt and selenium.
Which micronutrient is most deficient in Indian soils?
Among micronutrients, zinc, followed by boron. Sulphur, a secondary nutrient, is even more widely short.
Can NPK alone give a good crop?
Only if the soil supplies enough of every other nutrient. Where a micronutrient is short, more NPK does not lift the yield.
How do I know which micronutrient my crop needs?
Read the leaf symptoms, rule out pests and disease, and confirm with a soil and leaf test.

Micronutrient deficiency symptoms: how to read the leaves

Start with where the symptom appears. Nutrients that move in the plant (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium, molybdenum) show on old leaves first. Nutrients that do not move (iron, zinc, manganese, copper, boron, calcium, sulphur) show on young leaves, tips, flowers or fruit. Then look at the pattern and colour, rule out pests, disease, water and weather, and confirm with a soil or leaf test.

Step 3: rule out the look-alikes
Sucking pests and mites: check the underside of leaves with a hand lens.
Viruses: mosaic patterns, curling and stunting that spread plant to plant.
Fungal and bacterial disease: spots with rings or margins, rotting, a spreading pattern.
Herbicide drift: sudden damage along the field edge or in the wind direction.
Waterlogging, drought, cold and heat: the whole field changes after the weather does.
Root damage from nematodes, termites or root rot: lift a plant and check the roots.
Step 4: confirm before you spend
A soil test shows what the soil can supply. The Soil Health Card test covers zinc, iron, manganese, copper, boron and sulphur.
A leaf test shows what the crop actually took up.
A strip test: spray one nutrient on a few rows and compare the new growth after one to two weeks.
Keep photos with dates so you can compare later.
Taking a useful photo for advice
Photograph a whole plant, then a close-up of the worst leaf, both sides.
Show the youngest and the oldest leaves.
Add a photo of the field to show the pattern.
Send it to us on WhatsApp with the crop, age and recent fertilizer and spray history.

How can I tell which nutrient is deficient from the leaves?
First check whether old or young leaves show it, then the pattern and colour. Use the table on this page, rule out pests and disease, and confirm with a soil or leaf test.
Can two deficiencies show at the same time?
Yes, and it is common in Indian soils. The symptoms mix, so testing is the reliable way to know.
Do deficiency symptoms go away after treatment?
Leaves already damaged usually stay marked. The new growth after correction shows whether the treatment worked.

Zinc (Zn) in crops: role, deficiency signs and how to correct it
What zinc does in crops, how a shortage looks in each crop, why it happens, what it costs if ignored, and how growers confirm and correct it.

Zinc is a micronutrient the crop needs for its growth hormone (auxin), for more than a hundred enzymes, for chlorophyll and for healthy pollen. A zinc-short crop has small, narrow, pale new leaves, short internodes and poor tillering or flowering. Zinc is the most common micronutrient shortage in Indian soils, especially in alkaline, calcareous and low organic matter fields.
What zinc does in the plant
How zinc moves in the plant
Signs of zinc deficiency
Crop by crop
Where and why it happens
How it works with other nutrients
What happens if it is not managed
How to confirm it
How to correct it
Too much zinc
What zinc does in the plant
Helps the plant make auxin, the hormone that drives cell growth and normal leaf size.
Switches on many enzymes for energy, protein building and sugar use.
Needed for chlorophyll formation, so the leaf stays green.
Keeps cell membranes healthy, which helps roots hold nutrients and resist stress.
Supports pollen and seed formation, so it matters at flowering and grain fill.
How zinc moves in the plant

Zinc moves only a little inside the plant, so a shortage shows first on young and middle leaves. Once a leaf is formed short of zinc, it does not recover; only the new growth after correction looks normal.
Signs of zinc deficiency
Pale or yellow patches between the veins of young leaves, while veins stay green.
Small, narrow leaves, often bunched at the tip (little leaf or rosetting).
Short internodes, so the plant looks stunted and bushy.
Rusty brown spots on older leaves of paddy a few weeks after transplanting.
A white or pale band on both sides of the midrib in young maize leaves.
Delayed flowering and maturity, poor grain filling.
Crop by crop
What a shortage looks like
Khaira disease: rusty brown spots and stunting two to four weeks after transplanting, uneven patches in the field.
White bud: a broad pale band on each side of the midrib on young leaves, short plants.
Wheat
Grey-green or pale patches in the middle of leaves, uneven growth, poor tillering.
Mottle leaf: yellow patches between green veins, small pointed leaves, rosettes at shoot tips.
Small thick leaves, bronzing and short internodes.
More crops and look-alikes: Zinc deficiency symptoms crop by crop.
Where and why it happens
In India, an ICAR survey of more than two lakh soil samples found 51.2% of soils short of zinc, counting hidden shortages.
Alkaline and calcareous soils, common in Saurashtra and much of Gujarat.
Soils low in organic matter.
Fields where the topsoil was removed in land levelling.
Heavy, repeated use of phosphate fertilizers such as DAP.
Flooded paddy soils.
Cold, wet weather early in the season, which slows root uptake.
Sandy soils that are low in zinc to start with.
How it works with other nutrients
High phosphorus can lower zinc uptake, so DAP-heavy fields often show zinc shortage.
In high pH and calcareous soils zinc becomes less available.
Very high zinc can lower iron uptake.
Nitrogen raises the crop's need for zinc, so a well-fed crop shows zinc shortage sooner.
See nutrient interactions.
What happens if it is not managed
Stunted plants and fewer tillers or branches.
Late and weak flowering, poor fruit and grain set.
Lower grain weight and a poorer harvest even when NPK was applied.
Grain and fodder with less zinc, which matters for people and animals who eat them.
See the full picture of what unmanaged shortages cost.
How to confirm it
Look at the youngest leaves first: small, narrow, pale leaves point to zinc.
Rule out pests, virus and herbicide drift, which can look similar.
Ask for a DTPA zinc soil test, which is part of the Soil Health Card test.
A leaf test at the right stage confirms what the crop actually took up.
Spray a small strip and compare the new growth after one to two weeks.
How to correct it
Soil application of zinc sulphate before or at sowing in deficient fields. Do not mix it with phosphate fertilizers in the same bag or tank.
Foliar spray of zinc sulphate or a chelated zinc on the standing crop for quick correction of new growth.
Zinc-coated urea or zincated fertilizers where available.
Seed or seedling root dip for crops where your agriculture department advises it.
Zinc solubilising bacteria and organic manure to free zinc already locked in the soil and keep it available.
Take the dose from your soil test report, the product label or your agriculture officer.
Too much zinc
Zinc excess is rare in fields. It can happen near industrial waste or after repeated heavy doses.
Too much zinc can cause iron shortage, seen as yellow young leaves.

What is the main sign of zinc deficiency?
Small, narrow, pale young leaves with short internodes. In paddy, rusty brown spots a few weeks after transplanting (khaira) are a classic sign.
Why is zinc deficiency common in Gujarat?
Many soils in Gujarat are alkaline and calcareous and low in organic matter. Zinc becomes less available in these conditions.
Can I mix zinc sulphate with DAP?
Avoid mixing them in the same bag or tank. Phosphate and zinc can react, and high phosphorus also lowers zinc uptake.
Is foliar or soil application better for zinc?

Soil application builds up the field for the season. Foliar spray corrects the new growth quickly. Many growers use soil application where a soil test shows deficiency and foliar spray to correct a standing crop.
How quickly does a zinc spray work?
New leaves formed after the spray are normal in size and colour. Old damaged leaves do not recover.

Iron (Fe) in crops: role, deficiency signs and how to correct it
What iron does in crops, how a shortage looks in each crop, why it happens, what it costs if ignored, and how growers confirm and correct it.

Iron is a micronutrient the crop needs to make chlorophyll and to run photosynthesis and respiration. An iron-short crop shows yellow young leaves with a fine net of green veins, and in severe cases the new leaves turn almost white. Iron shortage is usually not a lack of iron in the soil but iron locked up in alkaline, calcareous or waterlogged soils.
What iron does in the plant
How iron moves in the plant
Signs of iron deficiency
Too much iron
What iron does in the plant
Needed to make chlorophyll, though it is not part of the chlorophyll molecule.
Part of the proteins that carry energy in photosynthesis and respiration.
Needed in legume nodules for nitrogen fixation.
Part of enzymes that protect the plant from stress damage.
How iron moves in the plant
Iron does not move from old leaves to new ones, so the youngest leaves turn yellow first while older leaves stay green.
Signs of iron deficiency
Young leaves turn pale yellow while the veins stay green, giving a fine green net.
In severe cases young leaves turn white or papery, with brown dead patches.
Older leaves stay green.
Shoots grow weak and short; fruit trees show dieback of twigs.
Symptoms are often patchy, worst in low spots and wet parts of the field.
Groundnut
Bright yellow young leaves with green veins on calcareous soils, common in Saurashtra.
Yellow to white stripes on young leaves, worst in ratoon crops and after waterlogging.
Yellow young leaves with a green vein net, small fruit and twig dieback.
Grapes
Yellow new leaves at shoot tips, poor bunch set.
Pale young leaves and weak new shoots on alkaline soils.
More crops and look-alikes: Iron deficiency symptoms crop by crop.
In India, an ICAR survey of more than two lakh soil samples found 19.2% of soils short of iron, counting hidden shortages.
Calcareous soils with free lime, where iron is locked up by high pH and bicarbonate (lime-induced chlorosis).
Over-irrigated or waterlogged fields, where roots cannot breathe.
Irrigation water high in bicarbonate.
Very high phosphorus, manganese, copper or zinc.
Cold soil early in the season.
High lime and high pH are the main cause of iron chlorosis.
Excess phosphorus, manganese, zinc or copper can lower iron uptake.
Iron and manganese compete: correcting one heavily can show the other.
Good organic matter keeps iron in forms roots can use.
Less chlorophyll, so less food is made and growth slows.
Weak flowering and fruit set in fruit crops.
Fewer and weaker nodules in legumes, so less nitrogen fixed.
Small fruit and twig dieback in orchards that suffer year after year.
Check the youngest leaves: a yellow leaf with a fine green vein net points to iron.
Note whether the problem is worse in wet or low spots and after heavy irrigation.
A soil test for pH, free lime and DTPA iron helps; a leaf test confirms.
Spray a few plants with an iron product and see whether the new leaves green up.
Improve drainage and avoid over-irrigation first; waterlogging alone can cause iron chlorosis.
Foliar sprays of ferrous sulphate or chelated iron green up new leaves. More than one spray is usually needed.
In high pH soils, iron chelates made for alkaline soil hold iron available longer than plain ferrous sulphate.
Plain ferrous sulphate applied to calcareous soil is often locked up quickly, so it may not work.
Organic manure, compost and humic substances help keep soil iron available.
Too much iron
Iron toxicity happens in acidic, waterlogged paddy soils, where too much iron dissolves.
Paddy leaves turn bronze or orange-brown with brown spots, and roots are coated orange.

Why are the new leaves yellow but the old leaves green?
Iron does not move from old leaves to new ones. Yellow young leaves with green veins usually point to iron shortage.
My soil has plenty of iron. Why is the crop iron deficient?
In alkaline, calcareous or waterlogged soils, iron is present but locked up. The crop cannot take it up, so the problem is availability, not quantity.
Does ferrous sulphate in the soil work?
In calcareous soil it is often locked up quickly. Foliar sprays or iron chelates made for high pH soils usually work better.
Can overwatering cause yellow leaves?
Yes. Waterlogged roots cannot take up iron, so the crop yellows even when iron is present.

Manganese (Mn) in crops: role, deficiency signs and how to correct it
What manganese does in crops, how a shortage looks in each crop, why it happens, what it costs if ignored, and how growers confirm and correct it.

Manganese is a micronutrient the crop needs to split water in photosynthesis, to switch on enzymes and to build lignin, which strengthens cell walls against disease. A manganese-short crop shows pale areas between the veins of young leaves with broad green bands along the veins, often with small grey or brown spots. It is common in wheat on light, alkaline soils and after paddy.

What manganese does in the plant
Splits water in photosynthesis, releasing oxygen; without it photosynthesis slows.
Switches on enzymes for energy, nitrogen use and growth.
Helps build lignin, which strengthens cell walls and roots against fungal attack.
Supports root growth and seed formation.
How manganese moves in the plant
Manganese moves little inside the plant, so young and middle leaves show the shortage first.
Signs of manganese deficiency
Pale green to yellow areas between veins of young and middle leaves, with broad green bands along the veins.
Small grey, brown or dead spots on the pale areas.
Weak, limp plants that look tired in the afternoon.
In wheat and oats, grey streaks or specks on leaves.
Poor grain filling.
Pale stripes between veins and grey-brown specks on middle leaves, common on light soils after paddy.
Pale areas between veins with broad green bands, a softer pattern than zinc or iron.
Pale stripes between veins of young leaves.

Soils rich in free lime.
Wheat after paddy, when the soil dries and manganese turns unavailable.
Over-limed acid soils.
Dry, well-aerated soils during cool weather.

Sulphur (S) in crops: role, deficiency signs and how to correct it
What sulphur does in crops, how a shortage looks in each crop, why it happens, what it costs if ignored, and how growers confirm and correct it.

Sulphur is a secondary nutrient the crop needs to build proteins, to make oil in oilseeds, to form chlorophyll and to use nitrogen well. A sulphur-short crop turns pale yellow from the young leaves, including the veins, and grows thin and weak. Sulphur shortage is the most widespread nutrient shortage in Indian soil tests, partly because urea and DAP carry no sulphur.

How sulphur moves in the plant
Sulphur moves only slowly from old leaves, so the shortage usually shows on young leaves first, unlike nitrogen, which shows on old leaves.

Why is sulphur deficiency so common in India?
Urea, DAP and MOP carry no sulphur. As they replaced single superphosphate and ammonium sulphate, and less manure was used, sulphur ran short. Soil tests show it as the most widespread shortage.
How do I tell sulphur from nitrogen deficiency?
Sulphur yellows the young leaves, including the veins. Nitrogen yellows the old leaves first.
Which crops need the most sulphur?
Oilseeds such as mustard, groundnut and soybean, pulses, onion and garlic.
Is gypsum a good sulphur source?
Yes. It supplies sulphur and calcium and suits most soils.

Silicon (Si) in crops: role, deficiency signs and how to correct it
What silicon does in crops, how a shortage looks in each crop, why it happens, what it costs if ignored, and how growers confirm and correct it.

Silicon is a beneficial element: not essential for all plants, but strongly useful for rice, sugarcane, wheat and many other crops. Plants lay it down as silica in their cell walls, which strengthens stems against lodging, toughens leaves against stem borers, planthoppers and fungal diseases, and helps the crop cope with drought, salt and heavy metals. Intensive rice and sugarcane cropping removes large amounts from the soil.

Strengthens stems and leaves, so crops lodge less.

Keeps leaves upright, so more light reaches the canopy.
Reduces water loss and helps under drought.
Lowers the harm from salt, iron, manganese and aluminium toxicity.
How silicon moves in the plant
Silicon is laid down as silica where water leaves the plant, in leaves, stems and husks, and does not move again.

Cobalt (Co) in crops: role, deficiency signs and how to correct it
What cobalt does in crops, how a shortage looks in each crop, why it happens, what it costs if ignored, and how growers confirm and correct it.

Cobalt is a beneficial element. The plant itself is not shown to need it, but the Rhizobium bacteria in legume nodules do: they need cobalt to make vitamin B12, without which they cannot fix nitrogen. A cobalt-short legume looks nitrogen-starved, with pale leaves and poor nodules. Cobalt in fodder also matters for cattle and sheep, which need it for their own vitamin B12.
